name: Sulfacetamide

lead: Sodium sulfacetamide is a sulfonamide antibiotic applied to the skin, often combined with sulfur, in prescription lotions and washes for acne, rosacea with bumps and seborrheic dermatitis. People use it for clearer, less red skin.

It blocks bacterial folic acid synthesis to slow bacterial growth, and sulfur adds a keratolytic (skin-shedding) effect. Together they calm inflamed skin and reduce breakouts. The sources reviewed describe its role rather than citing trial results.

paras: It is used as a leave-on lotion or a wash on a routine set by a prescriber, often alongside other skin treatments.

Mild stinging, dryness and irritation are most common. The US label warns of Stevens-Johnson syndrome in sulfonamide-sensitive people and reports of drug-induced lupus, including one fatal case. People allergic to sulfa drugs should avoid it. Prescription product in the US.

angle.text: Sulfacetamide, usually combined with sulfur, works through antibacterial and skin-shedding action to calm inflamed skin, giving fewer breakouts and less redness. It is a prescription lotion or wash for acne, rosacea and seborrheic dermatitis.

lead: Sulfacetamide is a sulfonamide antibiotic used on the eyes and skin.[1][2] In dermatology it is most often sold as sodium sulfacetamide, frequently combined with sulfur, for acne vulgaris, rosacea with papules and pustules, and seborrheic dermatitis.[3][2] These conditions show on the face as inflamed bumps, persistent redness, flaking and scaling around the nose, brows and hairline, so people use the lotions and washes to get clearer, calmer, less flaky skin.[4][5]

The topical forms are lotions, washes and cleansers, with 10 percent sulfacetamide and 5 percent sulfur a common pairing; brand names include Klaron, Ovace, Plexion, Clenia, Avar and Prascion.[1][2] A 2005 evidence-based dermatology review states that topical sulfur/sodium sulfacetamide, along with oral tetracycline, topical metronidazole and topical azelaic acid, has been validated for rosacea by more than one randomized controlled trial.[6]

A review of topical acne agents and the US product label describe it as a prescription topical option; reported hypersensitivity is uncommon, but the label carries warnings about Stevens-Johnson syndrome in sulfonamide-sensitive people.[3][7]
infobox: Klaron, Ovace, Plexion, Clenia, Avar, Bleph-10 [2]
Half-life about 7-12.8 h; mostly excreted in urine[2]

paras: The US label for sodium sulfacetamide with sulfur indicates it for topical control of acne vulgaris, acne rosacea and seborrheic dermatitis. [7] Wikipedia notes the sulfur combination is commonly promoted for rosacea with papules or pustules, with sulfur acting as a keratolytic. [2] Common product concentrations are 10% sulfacetamide, often with 5% sulfur, as lotions, washes or cleansers. [1]

A review of seborrheic dermatitis lists sodium sulfacetamide among broadly used therapies, alongside coal tar, salicylic acid, selenium sulfide and antifungals, noting the condition is linked to Malassezia and inflammation.[5] Reviews of rosacea management place sulfacetamide/sulfur among topical medications such as azelaic acid and metronidazole, used alone or with oral antibiotics or light therapies.[4][8]

Rosacea is described in a 2022 comprehensive review as a chronic facial disorder with transient or persistent erythema, telangiectasia and inflammatory papules and pustules, affecting up to 10 percent of the world population and most often fair-skinned people aged 35 to 50; the review names topical azelaic acid, metronidazole and sulfacetamide/sulfur, oral tetracyclines and oral retinoids as the mainstay of treatment, alone or combined, with light therapies for the erythemato-telangiectatic type.[4] A 2016 review lists sodium sulfacetamide among topical remedies for the papulopustular type and says flushing is better prevented than treated, by avoiding triggers, moisturising and blocking UV light.[8]

A 2019 review describes seborrheic dermatitis as a chronic, recurring inflammatory disorder with erythematous patches and scaling in seborrheic areas including the scalp and face, usually in response to Malassezia species; the authors say treatment aims to clear signs, relieve itch and maintain remission, and that antifungal and anti-inflammatory agents are most common, with sodium sulfacetamide among other broadly used therapies.[5]
It is also used in eye drops and ointments for bacterial conjunctivitis. [1][2]

A 1976 controlled study of 95 patients with perioral dermatitis found consistent clearing with oral tetracycline combined with a topical sodium sulfacetamide-sulfur-hydrocortisone lotion, and found differences in cosmetic product use between patients and controls.[9] Wikipedia also lists research interest in pityriasis versicolor and blepharitis.[2]

Sulfacetamide appears in topical lotions, creams, washes and cleansers, ophthalmic drops and ointments, and combination products. Wikipedia lists Klaron and Ovace as 10 percent lotions, Clenia, Prascion, Avar and Plexion as 10 percent sulfacetamide with 5 percent sulfur, Bleph-10 as eye drops and Blephamide as the prednisolone combination for the eye.[2] The sodium salt is the form used because of its water solubility.[1] A 2003 review of topical acne agents groups sulfur and sodium sulfacetamide with benzoyl peroxide and salicylic acid as agents available in concentrations of 2 percent or more in over-the-counter acne treatments and some prescription products, all showing some percutaneous absorption.[3]
In the United States the sulfur combination is sold by prescription.[7]

Sulfacetamide belongs to the first antibacterial class, the sulfonamides, introduced in the 1930s after the discovery of Prontosil, and was one of the early derivatives developed for better solubility and lower toxicity than sulfanilamide, per Grokipedia.[1] Its sodium salt became widely used for topical and eye applications. The perioral dermatitis report of 1976 shows the sulfur-sulfacetamide lotion in dermatologic use by then,[9] and the combination had controlled evaluation in the 1990s.[10]

The most common effects are local stinging, burning, irritation, dryness and peeling. [2][1] The label says irritation and hypersensitivity reports are uncommon, but notes Stevens-Johnson syndrome has occurred with sulfonamides including topical sodium sulfacetamide, and that drug-induced systemic lupus erythematosus from topical use has been reported, in one case fatal. [7] Products are not for people sensitive to sulfur or sulfa drugs. [2]

Other reported effects include nausea, dizziness, tiredness and headache; serious allergic reactions and erythema multiforme are described, and one case linked eye drops to toxic epidermal necrolysis.[2]

A 2003 review of topical acne drugs reported that, other than skin irritation, only rare local and systemic hypersensitivity reactions to sodium sulfacetamide have been described, and that such agents remain largely unregulated at over-the-counter concentrations.[3] Wikipedia advises storing the compound away from light, since it is more toxic in light.[2]
Sulfacetamide competes with para-aminobenzoic acid and inhibits dihydropteroate synthase, blocking bacterial folic acid synthesis and slowing growth (bacteriostatic). [2][1]

Wikipedia describes it as bacteriostatic against many gram-positive and gram-negative bacteria, with resistance to one sulfonamide generally implying resistance to all. Oral absorption is reported as complete, protein binding 80 to 85 percent, and half-life 7 to 12.8 hours, with liver metabolism to inactive products and urinary excretion.[2] It is more toxic in light and is stored away from it.[2]

Sulfacetamide is a benzenesulfonamide with an amine group on the benzene ring, a white powder with formula C8H10N2O3S and molar mass 214.24 g/mol; it resists biodegradation and persists in surface water, and environmental toxicity studies of sulfonamides examine it among other compounds.[2][11]

In the US the sulfur combination is a prescription product.[7] It is not a prominent topic in looksmaxxing forums; it reaches patients mainly through dermatology prescriptions for acne, rosacea and seborrheic dermatitis. Brand names include Bleph-10 for eye drops and Blephamide when combined with prednisolone.[2]

Controlled studies of sulfacetamide-based products include a 1976 trial in perioral dermatitis,[9] a 1997 controlled report on sodium sulfacetamide/sulfur lotion,[10] and randomised trials in conjunctivitis comparing topical sulfacetamide with oral erythromycin for neonatal chlamydial conjunctivitis[12] and three topical antimicrobials in acute bacterial conjunctivitis.[13] A review of evidence-based dermatology states the sulfur/sulfacetamide combination has been validated by more than one randomized controlled trial for rosacea.[6]

A 1976 controlled study of 95 patients with perioral dermatitis tested oral tetracycline together with a topical sodium sulfacetamide-sulfur-hydrocortisone lotion and reported consistent clearing.[9] The 1997 letter on sodium sulfacetamide/sulfur lotion reported on a controlled clinical trial of the lotion.[10] In conjunctivitis, trials compared topical sulfacetamide with oral erythromycin in neonatal chlamydial conjunctivitis and with other topical antimicrobials in acute bacterial conjunctivitis.[12][13]
